Gold stocks vs. ETFs vs. gold-backed crypto

"Gold exposure" gets used as if it's one thing. It isn't. A mining stock, a gold ETF, and a gold-backed token can all show the same red streak on GoldAlert's board and still mean three very different things.

Spot gold: the reference point

Spot gold is the benchmark everything else gets compared to — the price for immediate wholesale delivery. Almost nobody trades at exactly that price, though. A retail buyer pays a dealer premium on top, and if you're holding physical metal, storage and insurance are yours to arrange and pay for.

Mining shares: gold with a company attached

AngloGold Ashanti, Gold Fields, Kinross, Harmony — these move with the gold price, but not only with the gold price. Production costs, debt, currency exposure in whichever country they operate, political risk, a mine safety incident, an earnings miss: any of these can send a miner's share price the opposite direction from gold itself. A red streak here doesn't necessarily mean gold is under pressure. Sometimes it just means one company had a bad quarter.

ETFs: two very different flavors

GLD holds actual bullion and tracks the metal fairly directly. GDX holds a basket of mining companies and behaves more like the mining sector than like gold itself — fees, liquidity, and what's actually inside the fund all differ between the two. A mining ETF is not a shortcut to owning gold; it's a shortcut to owning miners.

Gold-backed tokens: gold plus a few extra layers

PAXG and XAUT are built to track an ounce of gold each, held by the issuer. That's the pitch. What it adds on top of gold's own price risk is issuer risk, custody risk, blockchain and smart-contract risk, and exchange risk — real considerations, not just fine print. Some smaller gold tokens trade on one or two thin exchanges with inconsistent pricing; that's exactly why this simulator only tracks tokens with deep, verifiable liquidity across major venues.

Why the comparison chart rebases to 100

Gold at $4,000 an ounce and a $50 ETF share can't be lined up on the same axis without one dwarfing the other. GoldAlert's comparison tool rebases both series to 100 at the start of the range, so what you're looking at is relative performance, not a chart where one line is invisible next to the other.

The practical takeaway

Before trusting a red streak, ask what kind of asset it's on. Spot gold pulling back tells a broad-market story. A single miner pulling back might just be that company's news. Check the chart, the recent headlines, and the backtest — the signal is a starting point for research, not a substitute for it.

Always read the prospectus, token terms, or company disclosures relevant to the instrument you're considering. This is not investment advice.
